description: Echo Foundry Archive is building an interactive digital museum for the NASA Space Apps Challenge: "Abandoned but not Forgotten." We combine self-made sketches with official NASA open data, imagery, and historical research. Leveraging modern web tech and artificial intelligence, we preserve the legacy of silent deep-space explorers so their missions are never forgotten.
summary: Lunar-Martian Museum is a free web museum, with a Spanish/English switch, that tells the stories of NASA missions that have gone silent on the Moon and Mars. Visitors choose the Moon, Mars or all missions, browse 12 exhibits, and open a fact sheet with launch and landing dates, status, objective, coordinates and a photo. Every exhibit links to an official NASA source. The project addresses the challenge “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” by gathering scattered mission data into one clear place, so students and curious people can discover and remember these machines. It matters because it keeps the history of space exploration accurate, accessible and open to everyone, even on older computers
details:
What it does: Lunar-Martian Museum presents NASA’s silent lunar and Martian missions as museum exhibits. Each mission has a card with a photo, dates, status, coordinates and a short story, and a full fact sheet that opens on click.

How it works: Visitors filter by Moon, Mars or all missions, open any exhibit, enlarge its photo, and follow a link to the official NASA source. A button switches between Spanish and English.

Benefits and impact: It brings together mission information that is spread across many pages and makes it easy to read for students and curious people. It runs in any browser, even on older computers, because it does not depend on heavy 3D graphics.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript; hosted on GitHub Pages; built with the help of an AI coding agent (Hermes) and AI assistants.

Creativity: Instead of a plain list, the project treats each mission as an exhibit in a museum, following the theme “Abandoned but not forgotten.”

Factors considered: Accuracy (every exhibit links to an official NASA source), accessibility (simple code, works on low-end devices), language access (Spanish and English), and crediting NASA as the source of data and images. The project was built by one participant.

AI disclosure: The website code was created with AI assistance. The mission research and sources were gathered and reviewed by the participant.
